sections.html:
• Name: Bumble bee shrimp (Striped Bumble Bee Shrimp, Striped harlequin, Zebra shrimp – Gnathophyllum americanum; Spotted Bumble Bee Shrimp – Gnathophyllum elegans)
  • Minimum tank size: 10 gallons (~40 litres)
  • Breeding: Difficult (almost impossible)
  • Water type: SG 1.023–1.025
  • KH: 8–12
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: carnivorous
  • Temperament: territorial
  • Life span: up to 2 years
  • Colour: dark and white stripes, or yellow dots all over the body

Bumble bee shrimp are distributed mainly in the eastern Atlantic. They are also known from Bermuda, India (Landfall Island, North Andaman), and from the Indo-West Pacific region from the Red Sea to Japan, Australia and Oceania.

Gnathophyllum is a group of marine crustaceans that live in the shallow waters of tropical and subtropical seas.

They are often found on rocky and coral reefs as free-living shrimp, or in association with echinoids, ophiuroids, sea stars and sea cucumbers in intertidal pools. They are also known to be associated with coelenterates, echinoderms and the echinoid Echinometra lucunter, where they presumably find shelter, although there is no certainty about possible commensalism in Gnathophyllum species. They are found free-living and on a wide array of substrates (hard natural, hard anthropogenic, and amidst algae), suggesting that their body colour pattern is not particularly related to any habitat type.

Because of their small size there are no minimum requirements. Even a 10 gallon (40 litres) tank is good enough for a few Bumble bee shrimp.

A larger tank is much better for the stability of water chemistry. The only problem is that these little shrimp may get lost in large tanks, so you may see them only about once a month.

Keeping Bumble bee shrimp in an aquarium is not complicated because they have no special water quality requirements. They should be kept under conditions suitable for any other typical reef-aquarium inhabitants.

They need careful acclimation, as all invertebrates do, and it should be done very slowly; 2–3 hours is generally good enough. They do not like swings in salinity.

Tank décor should include plenty of structures for the shrimp to hide in. If the conditions are met, they will show funny behaviour and make periodic trips to the front glass.

• Temperature: 22–26°C
  • pH: 8.1–8.4
  • Hardness: 8–12 dKH
  • Calcium: 400–450 ppm is optimal, but it can be a bit lower or higher. Calcium, pH and alkalinity must be maintained at acceptable levels.
  • Salinity: SG 1.023–1.025
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm

Lighting: Bumble bee shrimp do not really need light, so lighting should be adapted to the needs of the corals and fish in the tank.

Substrate: These shrimp are not diggers and have no preference for the substrate.

The most challenging aspect of caring for Bumble bee shrimp is the feeding regime. They are carnivorous marine invertebrates and do not eat algae at all.

In the wild they prefer to feed on sea stars; to be precise, they eat the tube feet of echinoderms. Therefore Bumble bee shrimp should not be kept with most starfish, sea urchins, sea cucumbers and sand dollars, or they should be well fed to reduce the risk of aggression. There are some reports of consumption of other echinoderms even without tube feet, but these observations were usually recorded on starved specimens with no access to sea stars.

They do not require sea stars for survival. If sea stars are not present in the tank they will not starve to death (unlike Harlequin shrimp). Bumble bee shrimp will eat any frozen meaty foods (such as brine or mysis shrimp, cockle, or small pieces of fish or shrimp) that you feed them.

These shrimp are very bad at finding food, and it is recommended to feed them every day.

Until Bumble bee shrimp get used to the daily life of the aquarium they are very shy and easier to find at night when the lights go out. Through the day many like to sit under rocks or hide away from their tank mates. This lifestyle is probably due to their small size and the fact that many predators could take advantage of them.

In nature, Bumble bee shrimp are typically found in pairs, where males display a ritual dance by covering and shepherding the female with his claws. However, unlike their closest relative the Harlequin shrimp (Hymenocera picta), they do not show completely monogamous behaviour.

Although quite peaceful, they do not like the presence of their own kind in the tank. Despite their small size they are territorial, but their territories are not big and they usually do not fight to the death.

Reef safety: In most cases there are no problems with Bumble bee shrimp in reef tanks and they will not harm corals. Only one case is known of them picking on Crocea clams; just do not let them starve.

Tankmates: Bumble bee shrimp do not bother other tankmates and usually come out right before the lights go off to find food. The ideal situation is a species tank, but they can be kept with other fish if chosen with care. They are small and prone to being eaten by many carnivorous fish; large predators such as triggerfishes, wrasses, hawkfishes and angelfishes are not suitable. Avoid aggressive eaters and large or aggressive invertebrates such as Coral banded shrimp and Arrow crabs.

Potentially good tankmates: Boxer crabs, Emerald crabs, Porcelain anemone crabs, cleaner shrimp (Peppermint shrimp, Red Fire shrimp, Skunk Cleaner Shrimp, Red-white Cleaner Shrimp), Saron shrimp and Sexy shrimp usually do not bother Bumble bee shrimp.

The colouration depends on the species. Gnathophyllum americanum has a colour pattern of alternating transverse dark reddish-brown and white stripes; narrow transverse white bands are seen all over the carapace and abdomen (Striped Bumble Bee Shrimp). In Gnathophyllum elegans the adults have small yellow-orange spots (composed of smaller spots grouped together) scattered all over the body with no specific arrangement (Spotted Bumble Bee Shrimp).

There are no reports of Bumble bee shrimp breeding in captivity. Despite possible interest in exploiting these species in the marine aquarium trade, little is known about the larval, postlarval and juvenile stages of some species.

Females become mature when their carapace is around 2.3–4.4 mm. The larval development of this genus is poorly documented; so far only the first-stage zoea of Gnathophyllum americanum has been described.

Bumble bee shrimp are a small saltwater species, reaching a maximum size of about 2.5 cm (generally a little less, about 2 cm) in the aquarium. Their rostrum is so short and directed slightly downwards that they look as if they have no head. In fully mature adults the body is very stout and the abdomen is straight.

The colour pattern differs between early juveniles and adults: juveniles can have many stripes, blotches and dots, which start fading in late juveniles.

There is no official data on how long Gnathophyllum species live in the wild. In captivity they are believed to reach 2–3 years with good care.

Asterina starfish: There is a popular misconception that Bumble bee shrimp can control or eliminate Asterina starfish. Asterina starfish do not have tube feet, the shrimp would have to be really hungry, and in general they are not good hunters. To eliminate Asterina starfish, Harlequin shrimp are needed. There are many species of Asterina; some are coral safe while others can destroy a reef tank, and it is very difficult to tell which species you have. They also multiply very quickly, so if you see only one there are probably many others hiding.

Bumble bee shrimp should only be acquired if you are willing to give them special care and attention, since they cannot thrive on other food items nor survive in a tank full of aggressive tankmates.
